save_card.title: GLYBURIDE (THE LOW THAT COMES BACK)
items: Confused at night with diabetes? Glucose first
Awake and swallows safely: 15 g fast sugar, recheck in 15 minutes
Can't swallow safely: IV dextrose or glucagon, as ordered
Sulfonylurea lows last for hours: keep rechecking, report

memory_line: Confused with diabetes? Check the sugar first.
caption_lesson:
🌙 Night shift, 3:10 AM. She's 81 with type 2 diabetes.
• Took her glyburide with dinner, ate only a few bites
• Now: mumbling, sweaty, picking at the sheets

❌ 3 mistakes
1️⃣ Charted "sundowning", no glucose check
2️⃣ Orange juice when she couldn't swallow safely
3️⃣ One recheck, then walked away
➡️ 5:10 AM: glucose 31 mg/dL (1.7 mmol/L), a seizure. Rapid response.

💊 Glyburide (THE LOW THAT COMES BACK)
• A sulfonylurea: it makes the pancreas release insulin, whether she eats or not
• Its lows can last or come back for many hours
• Older adults: on the Beers list to avoid

✅ The right move
• New confusion with diabetes? Check the glucose first
• Awake and swallows safely: 15 g of fast sugar (about 4 oz or 120 mL juice), recheck in 15 minutes
• Drowsy or can't swallow safely: nothing by mouth. IV (intravenous) dextrose or glucagon, as ordered
• Then a meal or snack once she's awake, keep rechecking, report

🧠 Confused with diabetes? Check the sugar first.
share_line: 📤 Send this to the nurse who'd chart 'sundowning' without a glucose check.
sources: American Diabetes Association (ADA) Standards of Care in Diabetes 2026, Section 6: Glycemic Goals, Hypoglycemia, and Hyperglycemic Crises

rn_checks: Hypoglycemia treatment: 15 g fast-acting carbohydrate, recheck in 15 minutes, repeat if still low, then a meal or snack (ADA 2026 Section 6)
Unsafe to swallow: nothing by mouth; IV dextrose or glucagon (IM, subcutaneous or intranasal) as ordered
Sulfonylureas, especially glyburide, cause prolonged and recurrent hypoglycemia; Beers 2023 avoid list
